Under a stricter reading that required a non-underscored, book-level attribute, Swift would drop to 5/6 (80); that alternative is disclosed in limitations.

Zig.reasoning: All 6 indicators satisfied -> 100. Zig is one of only three toolchains here that ship their own C-header binding generator and could satisfy F5 by execution rather than by documentation (Zig's translate-c, Go's cgo preamble, C++'s and Swift's direct header import). Every indicator is backed by a host execution with exit status 0 and the expected output, plus the reference-manual citations for F3 and F6.

cross_language_consistency_note: All ten languages were scored against the same four frozen probes (FFI-1..FFI-4 in 05_standard_rubrics.json -> frozen_probe_sets), implemented from one language-neutral specification and one shared C side: a single probes/FFI-2/c/caller.c used unchanged for every language that produced a linkable artifact, and a single header-only probes/FFI-4/c/supplied.h used unchanged for every language that consumed a header. Every probe prints the same canonical strings, recorded in probes/EXPECTED_OUTPUT.txt, so 'passed' means byte-identical output for all ten: 'cos(1.0)=0.5403023059'; 'ffi2_add=42'; 'sizeof=16 offset=8' + the sorted doubles + the sorted records; 'supplied_add=42' + 'supplied_weighted=4.50' + 'SUPPLIED_SCALE=3'. FFI-3 was made uniform by routing every language through the SAME C function, libc qsort, which forces four things at once for everyone: a pointer+length array modified in place, an element size the language must compute, a mixed int32/double struct whose fields C reads at its own offsets, and a C-ABI callback back into the language. Each language additionally prints its own measured struct size and field offset, so 'C-compatible layout' is an observed 16/8 rather than an assertion. Every language was run under exactly the command frozen for it in rubric_verification_recipes.by_language, with no flag added or removed, in one final pass whose exit statuses are all recorded. Three interpretive rules were fixed BEFORE any language was scored and then applied to all ten without exception. (1) F3 is read as: the FFI mechanism(s) the probes actually use or attempt must be documented at that language's frozen official_docs_root, including the foreign-type-to-language-type mapping. This is what gives F3 to Python (ctypes fundamental-types table), Java and Kotlin (the Linker C-type/layout/carrier table), Swift (Apple's C-type aliases plus @_cdecl at docs.swift.org) and Quidra (the C FFI section of docs/spec/language.md), and what denies it to TypeScript, where no such mechanism exists to document. The alternative strict reading - that F3 fails whenever the F2 direction is unsupported - would have removed F3 from Python, Java, Kotlin and Quidra alike; it was rejected for all four together, not for any one of them. (2) F6's second conjunct is read as PRESENCE of the target/flag/feature in the installed toolchain, not successful end-to-end execution, because global_rules.tool_availability_states.scoring_effect enumerates the indicators that require successful execution (V3, V4, V5, Q2, Q3, Q4, F2, F4, F5, C1, C5, P3) and F6 is deliberately absent from that list. Presence was still evidenced by a host command for every language: an executed Objective-C++ program (C++), an emitted .wasm binary (Go, Zig), an instantiated and called wasm module (TypeScript), an executed Objective-C selector dispatch (Swift), executed JVM interop (Kotlin), the toolchain's own target list (Rust), and explicit negative commands for Python (no wasm platform, no relevant builtin), Java (java.scripting present but 0 engine factories) and Quidra (official docs state WASM is unimplemented). (3) A 'not installed and may not be installed' tool is NOT SATISFIED with availability_state S3 for every language equally: rust-bindgen for Rust and jextract for Java and Kotlin all fail F5 on identical grounds, and none of the three was rescued. Post-assignment cross-check: no two languages with the same observable evidence received different levels, and no two with different evidence received the same level. The four languages at 100 (C++, Go, Swift, Zig) are exactly the four that passed all four probes by execution AND reach a second ecosystem - the same evidence, the same level. Rust at 80 differs from them on exactly one observable, F5 (S3). Kotlin at 60 differs from Java at 40 on exactly one observable, F6, and that difference is substantive rather than definitional: the JVM is an additional ecosystem for Kotlin and is Java's own runtime. Python and Java both sit at 40 with different satisfied sets of the same size (F1/F3/F4 for both, in fact the identical set) - same evidence, same level. Quidra and TypeScript both sit at 0 with one indicator each, but for opposite reasons, recorded separately: TypeScript has no C FFI at all, while Quidra has a working, documented C FFI that this probe set nonetheless defeats. Zig's FFI-4 probe reads the translate-c output through probes/FFI-4/zig/ffi4_supplied.zig, a symlink to the build/ffi4_supplied.zig path that the frozen recipe writes. Zig refuses @import of a path outside the root module directory, and the frozen command may not be altered; the symlink surfaces the same generated file inside the module without changing the command or hand-writing any declaration.
limitations: F5 could not be executed for Rust (rust-bindgen), Java (jextract) or Kotlin (jextract). All three tools are admissible under the frozen rules - rust-bindgen is published by rust-lang, jextract by the OpenJDK project - but none is part of its language's installed distribution here and global_rules.host_verification.no_installation_of_extra_software forbids installing them. All three are recorded availability_state S3, verification_status unverified, NOT SATISFIED, exactly as tool_availability_states.scoring_effect.everything_else requires. This costs Rust 20 points and is a host-provisioning artefact, not a measured property of the language; it belongs in standard/rubrics/host_limited_indicators.json.

Rust's F6 rests on `rustc --print target-list` reporting eight wasm32 targets. An actual wasm build FAILS on this host because the Homebrew rustc repackage ships no precompiled core/std for wasm32 (availability_state S2; verbatim error recorded in Rust's evidence). Under a stricter reading of F6 that demanded a successful wasm build, Rust would fall to 4/6 and 60. The presence reading was chosen for the reason given in the consistency note and applied to all ten.

Swift's F2 mechanism is the underscored @_cdecl. The formalized non-underscored spelling (@c / @cdecl, SE-0495) is NOT available in Apple Swift 6.2.3 - both were tried and rejected with 'unknown attribute'. @_cdecl is named as the C-calling-convention export mechanism on docs.swift.org (a frozen Swift official_docs_root), but only on an Embedded Swift ABI page, and it is an underscored attribute that Swift's own reference guides describe as unofficial. Under a stricter F3 reading Swift would be 5/6 and 80. This is the single most contestable indicator in the metric.

Java's F6 was scored NOT SATISFIED. The java.scripting module IS present in the installed JDK 26, but it ships no engine (`new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineFactories()` returned 0 on this host), so no additional non-C ecosystem is actually reachable; Nashorn was removed in JDK 15 and the JDK exposes no WASM, .NET or Objective-C target. A scorer who counted the presence of the java.scripting module alone would give Java 4/6 and 60. The command and its output are recorded so the alternative is auditable.

C++'s F6 rests entirely on Objective-C++, which was compiled and executed here. The wasm route is NOT available to this toolchain: Apple clang 17 registers no WebAssembly backend (`clang --target=wasm32 -c` fails with 'No available targets are compatible with triple "wasm32"'). On a host with upstream LLVM rather than Apple clang, C++ would satisfy F6 by a second independent route as well.

Quidra's F1 failure is narrow and is reported as such rather than as an inability to call C. `quidra 0.2.0` reserves the C symbol `cos` in its runtime-prelude list (src/checker.cpp), so the frozen probe cannot bind it; a supplementary, clearly-labelled non-probe execution binding the unreserved libc symbol `acos` succeeded, proving the FFI mechanism itself works against the host C library. The documented workaround - 'use a distinct C wrapper symbol' - cannot be applied with first-party flags because `quidra build` accepts no object, library or linker input (`-lm` -> 'unknown build option'). The supplementary run was NOT counted toward any indicator.

FFI-1 through FFI-4 give no credit for FFI ergonomics, safety, or performance, and no partial credit within a probe. A language that passes a probe barely and one that passes it idiomatically score identically, by design of the frozen rubric.

Only E1 and E2 were consulted, as this metric's evidence_sources specify. No E3-E7 evidence was used for any language, so no language was advantaged or disadvantaged by repository, package-index or adoption evidence here.

The probe sources, the shared caller.c and supplied.h, the expected-output file and the full command/exit-status log now live under standard/rubrics/probes/ and were all written before any language was scored; the evidence-collection order placed Quidra last, per global_rules.evidence_collection_order.
